metadata.title: Comparing parental and school pressure in terms of their relations with students' well-being

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PIRLS 2021 Germany field test data collected in early 2020, with a stratified school selection procedure (including proportion of students with an immigration background) and random selection of classes within schools. The analytic sample comprises 342 fourth graders from 17 classes in 17 schools across three German federal states; one class was excluded from self-report measures due to early termination, and additional students were excluded for disabilities, language barriers, or data backup failure. For the reading achievement outcome, the authors computed weighted likelihood estimates (WLE) from a 1-PL IRT model using PIRLS standard scaling procedures, and then standardized the WLE scores; this is a psychometric scaling step rather than an explicit complex-survey weighting variable applied in the SEMs. In the reported SEM analyses, the paper does not describe applying PIRLS sampling weights (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT) or replicate weights; instead, it accounts for clustering by using cluster-robust standard errors for students nested within classes and handles missingness within SEM using full information maximum likelihood (FIML).

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Participants were fourth graders in German elementary schools who participated in the PIRLS 2021 field test conducted in early 2020. Schools were selected using stratification characteristics (including proportion of students with an immigration background) to obtain a representative sample; within each school, classes were randomly selected. One class (n=25) terminated the test session before completing, leading to missing values on all self-report measures of interest; students with functional or intellectual disabilities or due to language barriers were excluded (n=6), and one additional student was excluded due to data backup failure. The final analytic sample therefore consisted of 342 fourth graders from 17 classes in 17 schools across three federal states. Missingness in the SEMs was handled with FIML, and the paper reports that missingness on academic pressure variables was relatively high (school pressure and parental pressure missing rates of 0.25 each) but did not differ by age/gender/socioeconomic status.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIRLS 2021 Germany Field Test Grade 4 Reading (WLE achievement; early 2020 administration)
main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM (cluster-robust SEs; FIML missing data). School pressure → satisfaction: β = -0.02, p = .822 (not significant). Parental pressure → satisfaction: β = -0.17, p = .047 (significant negative). In the combined model controlling for gender and academic achievement: school/parent pressure paths became statistically non-significant; academic achievement → satisfaction: β = 0.26, p = .009; gender → satisfaction not reported as significant in the combined model figure text. Additional analysis (Enjoyment of school (well-being facet)): SEM (cluster-robust SEs; FIML missing data). School pressure → enjoyment: β = 0.08, p = .477 (not significant). Parental pressure → enjoyment: β = -0.03, p = .377 (not significant). In the combined model: gender → enjoyment: β = 0.21, p = .002 (significant positive); academic achievement → enjoyment not reported as significant in the combined model text. Additional analysis (Worries about school (well-being facet)): SEM (cluster-robust SEs; FIML missing data). School pressure → worries: β = 0.27, p < .001 (significant positive). Parental pressure → worries: β = 0.26, p = .003 (significant positive). In the combined model controlling for gender and academic achievement: academic achievement → worries: β = -0.19, p = .010 (significant negative); pressure paths became statistically non-significant when both sources were included. Additional analysis (Physical complaints related to school (well-being facet)): SEM (cluster-robust SEs; FIML missing data). School pressure → physical complaints: β = 0.09, p = .469 (not significant in linear SEM). Parental pressure → physical complaints: β = 0.13, p = .037 (significant positive). Additional exploratory quadratic analysis (manifest variables): low school pressure reduced physical complaints up to a point, while high school pressure increased physical complaints (reported as negative linear and positive quadratic pattern). In the combined model: academic achievement → physical complaints: β = -0.34, p < .001 (significant negative); pressure paths became statistically non-significant when both sources were included. Additional analysis (Social integration (well-being facet)): SEM (cluster-robust SEs; FIML missing data). School pressure → social integration: β = -0.04, p = .660 (not significant). Parental pressure → social integration: β = -0.23, p = .045 (significant negative). In the combined model controlling for gender and academic achievement: pressure paths became statistically non-significant; academic achievement → social integration not reported as significant in the combined model text.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2021 Germany Field Test Grade 4 Reading the study leveraged school pressure, parental pressure, gender, and academic achievement (WLE) to predict satisfaction with school, finding that parental pressure was significantly negatively associated with satisfaction while school pressure showed no significant association. This indicates that reducing perceived parental pressure may support more positive school satisfaction among late elementary students, though the cross-sectional SEM design does not establish causality.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PIRLS 2021 Germany field test data from 342 fourth graders (17 classes in 17 schools across three federal states) collected in early 2020. Students’ reading achievement was scaled using a 1-PL model and summarized as standardized weighted likelihood estimates (WLE reliability = .86), while students’ school-related well-being was measured with five facets: satisfaction, enjoyment, worries, physical complaints, and social integration. The authors used SEM in R (lavaan) with cluster-robust standard errors for students nested within classes and handled missingness via full information maximum likelihood (FIML). In separate SEMs, school pressure significantly predicted worries (β = 0.27, p < .001) and parental pressure significantly predicted satisfaction (β = -0.17, p = .047), worries (β = 0.26, p = .003), physical complaints (β = 0.13, p = .037), and social integration (β = -0.23, p = .045). When both pressure sources were included simultaneously, pressure effects largely attenuated to non-significance, and academic achievement showed significant negative associations with worries and physical complaints. Limitations include the cross-sectional design (no causal inference) and the relatively high missing rates for pressure measures, plus the fact that SEM estimates are not ML predictive performance metrics.
